World.title: Lithium Before Democracy: A Serbian Strongman and His German Shadow
World.content:
In Serbia, Germans are sometimes referred to as Švabe, from the German Schwaben for natives of the historical Swabia region. It’s rude, but not as rude, say, as the term Kraut used by Britons, an unfortunate reference to the German liking for sauerkraut.

So it was indicative of their closeness that, in February 2023, Serbia’s president referred in public to Jörg Heeskens as moj Švaba, or ‘my Schwaben’.

“I call him my Švaba and he calls me ‘my wild Serb,’” Aleksandar Vucic said during the opening of a factory by the German tyre giant Continental in the northern Serbian city of Novi Sad. “That’s how we trade compliments.”

Vucic was thanking Heeskens for his contribution to the deal.

It was the kind of contribution Heeskens is paid to make from German public coffers, but while sitting in the same building as Vucic. And he’s been doing it for 13 years, through various iterations of Vucic’s role in running Serbia - from defence minister to deputy prime minister, prime minister and, since 2017, president of the republic.

As head of state, Vucic should play only a ceremonial role in Serbian public life. That’s what the Serbian constitution requires.

But Vucic has turned the constitution on its head, concentrating power in the office of the president, whether it’s on questions of foreign policy, defence, the economy or ribbon-cutting at a Continental tyre factory.

And none of those projects come bigger than a Rio Tinto lithium mine that Germany has been a powerful supporter of, coveting its output for the batteries needed to power the German car industry’s transition away from fossil fuels.

A trove of official documents from German authorities covering the period 2020-2026, obtained and analysed by BIRN and Der Spiegel over the course of six months, lay bare Germany’s behind-the-scenes maneuvering to get the mine underway in the face of widespread opposition from ordinary Serbians - and its disregard for Vucic’s subversion of democracy in the interest of getting it done.

At the centre of it all stands 49-year-old Heeskens, a ‘long-term expert’ formally employed by the German Ministry of Economic Affairs and Energy, who has Vucic’s ear, a Serbian side gig called Happy Hazelnuts, and an apartment worth at least half a million euros in an upscale, Dubai-style development in Belgrade mired in controversy since the builders first broke ground.

World.title: Turkish Journalists Protest Accreditation Denials for NATO Summit in Ankara
World.content:
NATO denied accreditation to dozens of Turkish journalists and media outlets on Wednesday that were intending to cover the alliance’s July summit in Ankara, drawing criticism from press freedom organisations over the lack of explanation for the decision.

Reporters Without Borders’ Turkey representative, Erol Onderoglu, said the decision effectively excludes a significant part of Turkey’s media from the event. “We struggle to understand this accreditation approach that closes the NATO summit to an important part of the Turkish media,” Onderoglu said on Thursday.

Criticising the lack of explanation and the absence of an appeal mechanism, he called for “a transparent accreditation process that respects journalists’ work and the public’s right to information”.

For the Ankara summit on July 7-8, the Turkish government is imposing strict security measures in and around the capital city. All gatherings and protests have been banned and all public workers sent onto a compulsory administrative holiday.

Accreditation requests from numerous Turkish media outlets, including Halk TV, Cumhuriyet, Sozcu, BirGun, Evrensel, Nefes, ANKA, Ilke TV and Medyascope, were rejected without explanation. All the barred news outlets and journalists are known to be critical and independent voices.

An email sent by NATO’s Accreditation Unit, seen by BIRN, told applicants that their requests for accreditation “cannot be granted”. The message added: “I cannot discuss the reasons for this decision, which is final.” It advises the journalists to follow publicly available sessions through NATO’s website.

“As a journalist who has followed NATO summits in Istanbul, Strasbourg/Kehl, Lisbon, Chicago and Brussels, along with countless NATO ministerial meetings and missions, I unfortunately will not be able to cover the summit being held in my own city, Ankara,” a senior Turkish security reporter, Duygu Guvenc, wrote on X.

The Progressive Journalists Association, PJA, said the decision reflected the Turkish government’s long-standing discriminatory accreditation policy towards critical and independent media, which now has been extended to an international summit.

“The failure to explain the rejections demonstrated arbitrary decision-making and political discrimination, undermining both press freedom and the public’s right to information,” the PJA said in a statement on Thursday. It called on international media organisations and journalists’ unions to speak out against what it described as an anti-democratic restriction on media freedom,

The decision comes against the backdrop of declining press freedom in Turkey. In Reporters Without Borders’ 2025 World Press Freedom Index, Turkey was ranked in 163rd place out of 180 countries, its second-lowest position since 2002. RSF said discriminatory practices targeting journalists and media outlets critical of the authorities, including denying or withdrawing press accreditation, had become commonplace.

World.title: Bosnia’s Return to Financial Crime ‘Grey List’ Will Hurt Economy: Experts
World.content:
Experts say that being put on the “grey list” will negatively affect Bosnia’s economy by worsening control and payment delays.

Sweden and Switzerland have already increased controls over transactions with Bosnia, which shows how quickly trust of international financial markets can be lost, and how slowly it is regained, a representative of the Foreign Trade Chamber of Bosnia and Herzegovina explained.

He warned that this situation sends a negative signal to international financial institutions, investors and partners, and creates a fresh obstacle on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s European path.

“There will be a significant slowdown in international financial transactions. In practice, this means additional controls and delays in payments and disbursements from and to Bosnia and Herzegovina, increased business costs and more difficult cooperation between domestic businessmen and foreign partners,” the representative of the Chamber explained.

“Exporters are particularly at risk, given that more than 73 per cent of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s total exports go to the European Union market,” he added.

The same representative pointed out that increased supervision of financial flows and extended payment deadlines reduce the competitiveness of domestic companies, increase business risks and can lead to contract termination and loss of markets.

“This is particularly problematic given that a stable financial system and the fight against money laundering are key conditions in the process of accession to the European Union,” he said.

Ordinary Bosnians will likely feel the negative consequences through rising prices of goods and services, a possible increase in interest rates, difficulties with international payments and disbursements, as well as slower remittances from abroad.

A disrupted investment environment could result in a decrease in foreign investment and a further weakening of the economy at a time when Bosnia needs new investments and strengthening economic growth in line with EU standards.

“What is particularly worrying is that the process of leaving the ‘grey list’ takes between two and four years, and that any potential return to this list would have long-term consequences that would be difficult and slow to remedy,” the representative of the Foreign Trade Chamber pointed out.

The Chamber urges competent institutions to take urgent measures to protect the economy, preserve financial stability and ensure the continuation of Bosnia’s European path in the interests of the economy and all its citizens.

BIRN previously reported that if Bosnia found itself back on the “grey list”, this could affect the disbursement of EU funds, including millions planned through the Growth Plan.

The EU Delegation to Bosnia has said it understood the political commitment of the domestic authorities to eliminate any strategic shortcomings planned through the Growth Plan.

“The European Union has provided significant technical assistance to Bosnia and Herzegovina in this area through EU-funded programmes and is ready to continue supporting Bosnia and Herzegovina in implementing the measures envisaged with the domestic Action Plan for FATF,” it said.

“Progress in implementing these reforms also contributes to the country’s progress on its European path,” the Delegation explained.

The Delegation urged Bosnia’s authorities to dedicate themselves to implementing necessary reforms also because of SEPA.

World.title: Would You Take the 14-hour Overnight Train to Split & Back?
World.content:
June the 26th, 2026 – A trip to the Croatian coast by train can be a bargain, if you have the patience for an unusually long journey. Would you embark on the 14-hour overnight train to Split and back?

What is it actually like to travel by Croatian Railways (HŽ) on one of the country’s longest routes, where the journey can stretch to more than 14 long hours?

Index reports that the overnight train connecting Split and inland Croatia offers an affordable alternative to buses and cars, but passengers should prepare for a very different kind of travel experience. The ride is slow, with long stretches of the journey moving at a crawl, and delays are common.

The route has become something of an adventure in itself. Passengers have reported packed carriages, uncomfortable conditions, and overnight journeys where some travellers ended up sleeping in corridors or on the floor when seats were unavailable.

Still, the price remains the biggest attraction. A return ticket can cost around €40, making it one of the cheapest ways to travel between eastern Croatia and Split. For comparison, a bus ticket on the same route can cost more while getting you there several hours faster.

The train does have its fans. Travellers can enjoy the constantly changing landscapes of Croatia, avoid driving, and turn the journey into a social experience, especially on overnight trips when the train takes on an almost festival-like atmosphere.

The verdict? It may not be the fastest way to reach the Adriatic, but for those who see the journey as part of the adventure, HŽ’s overnight ride to Split offers a uniquely Croatian travel story.

World.title: Croatia and Canada Strengthen Cooperation in Nuclear Energy
World.content:
June the 26th, 2026 – Croatia and Canada are set to deepen cooperation in the field of nuclear energy, with the two countries exploring opportunities for collaboration.

The two nations on each side of the vast Atlantic Ocean will seek deeper cooperation involving technology, expertise, and the peaceful use of nuclear power.

Poslovni reports that the very welcome partnership comes as both countries look to strengthen energy security and develop low-carbon energy solutions. Canada has long been involved in nuclear research and technology, including the development of CANDU reactor technology, while nuclear power remains an important part of Canada’s electricity mix.

The cooperation is expected to focus on knowledge exchange, technical expertise, safety standards, and potential future projects connected with nuclear energy. Similar international nuclear partnerships have increasingly included cooperation on research, regulation, training, and advanced reactor technologies.

For Croatia, the move comes as the country examines ways to strengthen its long-term energy independence and expand its role in the regional energy market. Nuclear energy discussions are closely linked to the future of the wider Central European energy system, where existing nuclear capacity and new technologies such as small modular reactors are gaining attention.

The Croatian-Canadian cooperation marks another step in expanding bilateral ties beyond traditional trade and diplomacy, with energy and technology becoming an increasingly important area of partnership.

World.title: Croatia Signs Deal to Recruit Workers from Uzbekistan
World.content:
June the 26th, 2026 – Croatia has officially put pen to paper and signed a deal that will allow them to recruit and import workers from Uzbekistan.

Croatia is preparing to open a new channel for foreign labour recruitment after the Croatian Employers’ Association (HUP) signed an agreement with the Employers’ Confederation of Uzbekistan to facilitate the arrival of workers from the Central Asian country.

Poslovni writes that this memorandum, signed by HUP’s Construction Employers Association and its Uzbek counterpart, establishes a framework for long-term cooperation aimed at bringing qualified workers to Croatia while creating a more structured and transparent recruitment process.

The agreement focuses particularly on the construction sector, where Croatian companies have been facing a growing shortage of labour. Workers from Uzbekistan are expected to undergo vocational training, gain qualifications aligned with European standards, and receive Croatian language preparation before arriving.

HUP said the partnership is intended to reduce reliance on informal recruitment channels by working directly with Uzbek institutions. The model is designed to lower costs for employers and protect workers from excessive intermediary fees.

Representatives from both sides described the agreement as more than a short-term response to labour shortages, saying it aims to create a sustainable system for legal and organised labour migration between Croatia and Uzbekistan.

Croatia has increasingly turned to foreign workers as demographic decline, emigration, and labour shortages continue to affect industries including construction, manufacturing, logistics, transport, tourism, and hospitality.

World.title: flydubai Cuts Flights to Zagreb and Dubrovnik
World.content:
June the 26th, 2026 – The previously popular flydubai cuts its flights to both Zagreb and Dubrovnik, leaving many concerned about the very future of any connection with Croatia.

Dubai-based airline flydubai has reduced the number of flights operating to Croatia, cutting services on routes connecting Dubai with Zagreb and Dubrovnik.

Poslovni reports that these latest changes affect travellers relying on direct links between Croatia and the Gulf, with fewer available flight options expected during the travel season. flydubai’s Zagreb service has previously operated as a direct connection from Dubai, while Dubrovnik has also been served as part of the airline’s seasonal network.

The reduction comes as airlines continue adjusting schedules due to demand, aircraft availability, and broader network decisions. Passengers booked on affected services have been advised to check their flight status and contact the airline regarding possible changes.

For Croatia’s tourism sector, which depends heavily on international air connectivity, fewer direct links to major markets such as the Gulf could create additional pressure, particularly for Dubrovnik during the peak summer months

World.title: Plitvice Lakes System Falls Victim to Cyber Attack
World.content:
June the 25th, 2026 – The gorgeous Plitvice Lakes National park system fell victim to a cyber attack, with tickets and shopping severely disrupted.

A cyber incident has disrupted operations at Croatia’s Plitvice Lakes National Park, causing major problems for visitors and staff. Index reports that all electronic payment systems have been affected, with some visitors unable to use bank cards and several shops and facilities forced to close or accept only cash.

The park’s management confirmed that a cybersecurity incident had occurred and said security protocols were activated. Specialists are working to restore affected systems and determine the cause of the disruption.

Visitors reportedly faced long delays and confusion as everyday services were disrupted. The full extent of the damage, including any potential financial losses, is not yet known.

The incident comes amid a series of cyberattacks affecting Croatian institutions and services in recent years, including attacks that have disrupted public-facing systems and caused payment or service interruptions.

World.title: Croatia Launches Campaign to Attract Last-Minute Tourists
World.content:
June the 25th, 2026 – With the main summer season approaching, the Croatia has launched a new promotional push aimed at attracting last-minute visitors.

The campaign focuses on markets where Croatia traditionally performs strongly, with the goal of reaching travellers who have not yet finalised their summer plans. Poslovni reports that tourism officials say last-minute demand remains an important part of the booking cycle, especially as some guests increasingly make decisions closer to their departure dates.

HTZ director Kristjan Staničić said that Croatia remains a highly sought-after destination, but that the focus is increasingly shifting towards extending the season beyond July and August and attracting visitors throughout the year.

The campaign promotes Croatia’s coastal destinations, experiences and travel offer, while targeting potential guests through digital advertising and international markets. Previous HTZ campaigns have focused on key European markets including Germany, Austria, the United Kingdom, Switzerland and Belgium.

Tourism authorities say interest in Croatia remains strong, with travellers showing continued demand for summer holidays as well as for trips outside the traditional peak period.

The move comes as Croatian tourism continues to adapt to changing travel habits, with the industry looking to balance the busiest months of the year with stronger pre- and post-season results.

World.title: Sarajevo-Ploče Train Returns, Tickets to Cost Around €15
World.content:
June the 25th, 2026 – The much loved Sarajevo-Ploče train will officially return as of tomorrow, with tickets costing around 15 euros.

A popular seasonal railway connection between Sarajevo and Ploče is returning this summer, once again linking Bosnia and Herzegovina’s capital with Croatia’s Adriatic coast.

The Sarajevo–Ploče–Sarajevo passenger train will operate from June 26 until the end of August, running on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. The train will depart from Sarajevo in the morning, with the return journey from Ploče scheduled in the evening.

The journey takes around three hours and 20 minutes, offering travellers a scenic route through the Neretva valley, including stops in places such as Mostar and Čapljina.

A one-way ticket will cost approximately €15, while return tickets will be available at a discounted price. Additional discounts will apply for certain groups, including students, pensioners, journalists and larger groups of passengers.

The railway link has become increasingly popular among both locals and visitors, providing an alternative way to reach the Adriatic coast without relying on road transport. The route has also been praised for its views, passing through some of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s most dramatic landscapes.

Tickets for the seasonal Sarajevo–Ploče service will not be sold online, according to railway officials.

World.title: Scientists Confirm: Shark Caught Near Rogoznica in 2023 was Great White
World.content:
June the 25th, 2026 – Scientists have confirmed that the large shark caught in waters near Rogoznica back in 2023 was a great white shark.

Scientists have confirmed that the shark caught near Rogoznica in 2023 was a great white shark (Carcharodon carcharias), one of the most recognisable and protected marine predators in the world.

Index reports that the young shark, estimated to have been around 1.5 metres long, was reportedly caught accidentally by fishermen, likely with a longline. Instead of reporting the discovery to authorities or scientific institutions, the fishermen appallingly photographed themselves with the animal and later sold it to a restaurant. Thankfully, punishment followed.

Marine biologists described the find as extremely valuable for research, since great white sharks are rarely recorded in the Adriatic Sea. Experts say the species does not permanently live in the Adriatic but occasionally enters the area, mainly in search of food such as tuna.

Scientists stressed that such discoveries should be reported to institutions such as the Institute of Oceanography and Fisheries, as every confirmed sighting provides important information about the species’ presence and movement in the Mediterranean.

The incident also renewed discussion about the protection of sharks in the Adriatic. The great white shark is a protected species, and experts have warned that declining shark populations make every individual important for conservation efforts.

Despite their fearsome reputation, researchers note that great white sharks do not typically attack humans as prey. The last recorded fatality involving a great white shark in Croatian waters occurred near Vis back in 2008 and was not deadly.

World.title: As settlers rampage, IDF soldiers accused of aiding violence, theft against Palestinians
World.content:
One bright morning in October, a dozen soldiers riding in several military jeeps rolled up to the Issa family home in the northern West Bank village of Sanur.

The troops hopped out of the vehicles and grabbed Tayir Issa and his son Jamal without explanation, handcuffing and blindfolding them. Soldiers proceeded to kick and shove Issa and his son onto the ground, pushing their heads into the dirt as they showered the pair with insults and epithets.

Meanwhile, other soldiers arrived in a large civilian cargo truck.

In extraordinary scenes captured on camera by an individual who filmed the incident, the soldiers, in full combat gear, can be seen wrangling the familyâs cattle into the truck via a makeshift ramp rigged up by the uniformed Israel Defense Forces troops.

Despite Tayir and Jamalâs repeated requests to speak with a senior officer or see a legal warrant for the seizure of the 14 cows, no such documentation was produced.

Get The Times of Israel's Daily Edition by email and never miss our top stories Newsletter email address Get it By signing up, you agree to the terms

Instead, the cattle were driven away by the soldiers.

The family has yet to recover their livestock, their primary source of income, and in all likelihood, they never will.

The cows were taken, the army eventually admitted, in response to a request from two radical settler activists who run illegal farming outposts in the Jordan Valley and had falsely claimed to own the animals.



It was one of numerous instances of IDF soldiers assisting settlers in seizing Palestinian livestock or showing a willingness to work with Israeli extremists carrying out even worse crimes.

Across the West Bank, observers say, extreme, and often violent, settler activism is now taking place with the protection, cooperation and sometimes active participation of IDF soldiers of different types.

Increasingly, the IDF is cooperating with the extremists who set up illegal farming outposts and stations soldiers in those outposts, who are deployed in situations of violence — or âfrictionâ as the army euphemistically calls it — that at least one outpost leader has described as a deliberate tool for displacing Palestinian communities.

This has generated a situation in which IDF soldiers are intimately involved in daily occurrences of extremist settler harassment, and frequently either turn a blind eye to such incidents or intervene on behalf of the settlers.

In the most troubling situations, some IDF soldiers participate in the violence itself, especially those mobilized in regional defense, or Hagmar, units, made up of reservist settlers who are tasked with operating in areas near their homes.

In a number of cases, the soldiers have themselves been extremist settler activists, who have used their army-issued rifles to fire on Palestinians.



In a written statement, the IDF said it “strongly condemns incidents of violence and crime and is responsible for maintaining security and public order in Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley,” referring to the West Bank.

“Its role is to protect all populations in Judea and Samaria, and the Jordan Valley, while implementing the decisions of the political leadership, all in accordance with the law, international law, and military orders,” the statement added. “All IDF service members, both regular and reserve, are fully committed to this.”

Cases of violence and theft were described as “irregular incidents” that were “thoroughly investigated and handled in accordance with the findings.”

Critics say, though, that while the army regularly probes allegations of wrongdoing, investigations rarely result in prosecutions or convictions.

In the Issa family case, because the theft was caught on tape, legal proceedings were able to expose the IDF’s role in the act, though justice has yet to be served.

Following a petition to the High Court of Justice in November 2025 by the Association of Civil Rights in Israel, the army admitted in a formal submission to the court in December that the officer who ordered soldiers to seize the cattle had done so âwithout authorityâ and that the seizure had therefore been âunlawful.â

Video footage of IDF soldiers unlawfully removing cattle from the Issa family farm in the West Bank Palestinian village of Sanur, October 10, 2025. (Courtesy)

The IDF claimed that the cattle had been taken âin the sincere beliefâ that the settlers owned the livestock, and said that since it was a case of theft, the claim should be handled by the police and not the army.

Since the IDF does not have the authority to investigate property claims, the army told the court, it could not fulfill the demands of the petitioners to return the livestock to the Issa family, passing the case to the police.



The police have yet to recover the cows for the Issa family.

The army added that it was still examining the claims of violence made by the Issa father and son.

The harassment of rural Palestinian communities

The explicit goal of the settler extremists who establish illegal outposts and engage in violence against rural Palestinians is to push them off the land they own, or otherwise control or use, as part of their broader project to assert Jewish control over the entire West Bank.

The Palestinian Bedouin have become a specific target for forcible population transfer efforts because they graze their livestock across large tracts of land in the West Bank and their communities stand in the way of a rapidly expanding network of Israeli settlements and illegal outposts.

The Bedouin are also especially vulnerable because many of their hamlets and homes lack any kind of building permit or zoning plan as required by the Israeli authorities who administer Area C of the West Bank, and are therefore illegal.

This makes it far easier for extremist activists to harass and terrorize them, and, once they flee, prevent them from returning.

Over the last three years, IDF forces have been repeatedly documented as either turning a blind eye to the harassment and violence by settler extremists against such communities or actively assisting them.

Under the Geneva Conventions and other international treaties, the IDF, as the occupying authority, is obligated to protect the local population, including preserving public order and preventing the destruction of their property. Forcing local populations off their land is also prohibited except as a temporary security measure.

Ras ‘Ein al-âAuja was a Bedouin community in the southern Jordan valley, but incessant harassment and violence by extremists who built illegal outposts close to the hamlet ultimately led to its total depopulation in January this year.



In one notorious incident in March 2025, dozens of settlers entered the hamlet and stole some 1,500 sheep and goats from the community, one of the largest such thefts of livestock to date.

Footage from Looking the Occupation in the Eye, a left-wing organization that publishes evidence of settler violence against Palestinians, showed a man in IDF fatigues and an IDF-issued assault rifle present in the village at the time, as well as activists asking military personnel in an IDF armored vehicle for help in stopping the theft, to no avail.

protective presence activists encounter an unprecedented event in a Palestinian shepherd community? They bravely film and talk to everyone they can to achieve justice. They couldn't stop the settlers from stealing 1,000 sheep – but they documented it. pic.twitter.com/qcXlXMxYt4 — ××¡×ª×××× ××××××© ××¢×× ××× (@Mistaclim) March 11, 2025

Ras ‘Ein al-âAuja had been the last Bedouin community remaining in the southern Jordan Valley.

According to the BâTselem human rights organization, 59 Palestinian communities, home to over 4,000 people, have been displaced since that date due to settler violence and harassment in Areas C and B of the West Bank. Another 500-odd Palestinians have been forced out of their homes in 16 partially displaced West Bank communities.

The kind of harassment and theft witnessed in Ras ‘Ein al-âAuja has been repeated across the West Bank, either with the same indifference shown by the IDF soldiers in the mass livestock theft incident, or with their active participation and assistance.

In another incident of livestock theft by settlers seemingly abetted by the army, IDF soldiers were caught on security camera footage accompanying settlers as they made off with 150 head of sheep from the hamlet of Khirbet al-Halawa in the southern West Bank one night in January this year.

The IDF claimed in response that the troops had been alerted to the theft of livestock from a Jewish shepherd by Palestinians. But as previously admitted by the IDF itself in the Issa family case, police actions such as property recovery are not within the military’s authority, especially without a lawful order, which was not presented in the Khirbet al-Halawa incident.

In a response to this article, the IDF said that incidents in which IDF soldiers “exceeded their authority” have been examined and “steps taken to prevent similar incidents in the future.” It also claimed that in some incidents of IDF involvement in the seizure of livestock, the actions were “carried out by the police in accordance with the law and with an IDF escort,” but did not say which incidents it was referring to.

Doron Meinrath, a longtime activist with Looking the Occupation in the Eye and a member of a so-called âprotective presenceâ squad in the Jordan Valley for several years, said he has repeatedly seen IDF forces participating in the harassment of rural Palestinian communities.

Protective presence units formed by various left-wing groups are active across the West Bank in trying to shield Palestinians from Israeli abuse.

In one incident Meinrath said he observed in June 2024, also in Ras ‘Ein al-âAuja, IDF and police forces raided the village following an accusation from Zohar Sabah — an extremist under indictment for assault against Israeli human rights activists and under sanction by the UK and other nations — that herders in Ras ‘Ein al-âAuja had stolen his sheep.

Police and IDF forces initially ransacked sheep pens and confiscated livestock based on Sabah’s claims, Meinrath said. The next day, an IDF officer and three soldiers returned with Sabah to conduct further searches. A short time later, they fired several rounds of tear gas at the hamlet without any apparent reason, according to video Meinrath filmed.

IDF soldiers fire tear gas towards the West Bank Palestinian village of Ras al-Ein Auja, June 22, 2024 (Courtesy Looking the Occupation in the Eye)

Soldiers, soldiers, everywhere

The apparent increase in cooperation of IDF soldiers in incidents of settler harassment and violence against Palestinians appears to be partly a function of the increasing diversity of the type of IDF forces present in the West Bank.

In a recent report on violence committed by IDF soldiers, the Yesh Din human rights organization noted that it is often difficult, if not impossible, to distinguish between a regional defense unit soldier, a member of an emergency response team, and a settler who independently decided to put on a uniform, and to know when the individual is on active duty or not.

Emergency response teams are composed of civilians who have volunteered to help guard the settlement where they live, and whose operations are authorized under a classified military order. Until October 2023, they were not permitted to wear military uniforms, but that restriction was lifted in the wake of the October 7 Hamas-led attack. Their mandate for operations is not known since it is regulated by the classified military order, but they do appear to operate at times beyond the boundaries of the settlements they are supposed to defend.

Some settlers are members of both an emergency response team and a Hagmar regional defense unit, causing even greater confusion as to their powers and authorities.

âIsrael consistently, and as a matter of policy, enables the deliberate blurring of lines between settlers and military forces and promotes violent actions against Palestinian civilians in the West Bank by militias working in the service of settlement interest,â Yesh Din alleged in a recent report.

According to Meinrath, the soldiers, of all types, are not neutral referees when confrontations erupt between extremists and Palestinians, but display a clear preference for the settlers, prejudicing their response regardless of who initiated the violence or the surrounding context.

âThere is no doubt that these soldiers feel more comfortable with the settlers than with human rights activists or Palestinians,â Meinrath told The Times of Israel. âThey chat with them, have coffee with them, soldiers will visit the farming outposts and ride on the settlerâs donkey.”

He noted that when soldiers are newly deployed to the area, they are often briefed by security coordinators from nearby settlements, who shape their understanding of local conditions. The coordinators operate under military authorization to secure settlements against threats and are armed by the IDF.

âThe IDF soldiers come [to a sector], they are there for a few months, they donât know the area, and they go and speak to the local security coordinator because he knows the sector better than them,â said Meinrath.

Often when activists call the IDF to report violence or harassment by settlers, a local security coordinator will turn up first, and then tell the local IDF force himself that everything is in order, despite the violence, Meinrath claimed.

On other occasions, the IDF unit dispatched to the area will either fail to stop the violence, fail to detain the settlers, or detain the Palestinians, even when the settlers initiated a confrontation inside a Palestinian dwelling.

Military harassment of rural Palestinian communities

As well as facing army-abetted settler violence, Palestinian herders and farmers in Area C have been detained or otherwise harassed by IDF forces following claims made against them by settlers and illegal outpost residents, similar to the Issa family incident.

Iris Gur, 61, has been volunteering with the left-wing Combatants for Peace organization in the West Bank for the last eight years, in particular in the northern Jordan Valley area.

She described one incident in March in which Ahmad Abu Muhsin, a Palestinian Bedouin shepherd from the hamlet of al-Farisiyah, was detained by IDF soldiers on private Palestinian land he rents, while a settler from a nearby illegal outpost was able to continue grazing his flocks on the same plot.

The IDF declined to respond on the record as to why Abu Muhsin was detained.

Gur said Abu Muhsin has been repeatedly harassed by local settler extremists with the cooperation of the IDF due to the location of al-Farisiyah, which she said the settlers are trying to depopulate.

The army in May confiscated vehicles belonging to Abu Muhsin, claiming they were used inside IDF firing zones, but it has failed to enforce the prohibition against settler activists setting up outposts and carrying out grazing activities within the same zones, according to a High Court petition filed by the Association for Civil Rights in Israel on behalf of Abu Muhsin and other residents.

In response to the petitions, the IDF said that the asset seizures had been conducted against property unlawfully used within firing zone 901, and that the assets could be recovered if the owners paid NIS 26,000 ($8,900) in seizure expenses. The army did not address the claims of discriminatory enforcement of the firing zone restrictions.

The IDF also frequently uses closed military zone orders — ad hoc closures imposed over entire Palestinian villages — that activists say stymie their efforts to protect Palestinians from settlers, apparently in violation of a recent High Court decision.

According to rights groups, closed military zone orders often facilitate settler violence, since the IDF will frequently detain civil rights activists defying the order and trying to assist the Palestinian locals, while failing to detain settlers who are also ignoring the order.

Gur said she noticed the practice became commonplace during the 2024 olive harvest season, when she said IDF soldiers came to stop Palestinian olive growers and Israeli volunteers from harvesting the fruit âthe minute we came there.â

Before the war that broke out following the October 7, 2023, Hamas invasion and massacre, activists only needed to perform their protective presence operations for shepherds going to pasture their flocks out in the open, Gur said. Since the war, volunteers were also being called to protect Palestinian homes as well.

âAfter October 7, the level of violence by soldiers and settlers became extreme very quickly. Since then, the free hand which the soldiers and settlers received has turned the violence into a daily event, day and night, extreme violence not only against the Palestinians but also against Israeli and international activists,â said Gur.

The IDF said in response that the army uses closed military zone orders “in accordance with the law and High Court decisions, and only in situations where there is a concrete concern over regional security or of a disturbance to the public order,” and said that any claims that such orders are used for other purposes “are without foundation.”

The IDF also said that olive harvesting in the West Bank was carried out without restrictions “in 95% of the territory.” It added that in situations where the olive grower is close to Israeli settlements the harvest must be coordinated “for the sake of the security of the parties,” and said there were similar arrangements for the plowing season.

Military – settler outpost symbiosis

According to Yehudah Shaul, co-director of the OFEK organization, which researches Israeli policy in the West Bank, in recent years the IDF has devoted greater resources to protecting settlers and settlement outposts.

While there is no hard data, government funding allocations in recent years, including for security equipment, show a marked uptick in support for both settlements and illegal outposts.

Shaul noted that many illegal settlement outposts have IDF soldiers assigned to guard them, often from the regional defense units staffed by local settlers established after October 7. The residents of many outposts have a direct line of communication with the local IDF unit in the sector to enable their defense, he said.

In many cases, the soldiers of the regional defense units are themselves residents of illegal farming outposts, or from nearby settlements.

And the outposts are very often forward posts for the extremists inhabiting them, to attack Palestinian communities.

In one incident caught on camera in October 2025, Ariel Dahari, a resident of the illegal outpost of Oz Yair in the central West Bank, bludgeoned 52-year-old Afaf Abu âOlia around the head with a club as she was harvesting olives on land outside Turmus Ayya where she lives.

Abu âOlia was knocked unconscious and sustained a severe head injury as a result of the attack, and was hospitalized for a week. Dahari was indicted on terror charges over the attack.

Shaul pointed to a recent report detailing comments by the head of IDF Central Command Maj. Gen. Avi Bluth, in which he criticized the establishment of wildcat farming outposts set up without the coordination of the military or state authorities, indicating that other farming outposts that are illegal under Israeli law are nevertheless being established in the West Bank in coordination with the IDF and local government.

All settlements require cabinet authorization, and any settlement, outpost, or farm that never received such authorization is illegal under Israeli law.

But an investigation published by the Kan public broadcaster in December cited a lieutenant colonel who had served in the IDFâs Central Command for years who alleged that the army began cooperating with the establishment of illegal farming outposts once Bluth was appointed commander in July 2024.

âStarting in July 2024, an organized mechanism began to be built for establishing farm outposts in coordination with Central Command. There are actual orders authorizing settlement on the ground â a structured, orderly process,â the officer, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told Kan.

The IDF Spokesperson’s Department, in response, did not deny the allegation, but said that Bluth “acts in accordance with the law, and according to the authorities laid out in his position, and every decision regarding the evacuation or approval of settlements is done in accordance with regulations, in cooperation with the political echelon or with its approval.”

The IDF and the Civil Administration of the Defense Ministry do remove some of the wildcat outposts that are established without coordination with local municipal authorities in the West Bank and other state agencies. But of the 185 illegal outposts established in the last three and a half years, the left-wing Peace Now organization estimates that fully 160 have been established with the cooperation of state or local authorities, and have therefore not been targeted for demolition.

As well as apparently assisting in the establishment of coordinated outposts, the IDF Central Command, together with the Defense Ministry, also coordinates with settlement municipal authorities to determine which illegal farming outposts are eligible for government-issued security and infrastructure equipment, such as all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), floodlights, night vision goggles, drones, communications equipment, camera posts, water tanks and generators.

A letter issued by the legal adviser to the Settlements and National Missions Ministry in November 2024 confirmed that IDF Central Command approves which illegal outposts can get security equipment.

Tens of millions of shekels’ worth of such equipment has been distributed by the Settlements and National Missions Ministry to the outposts under the current government.

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who has spearheaded the government’s massive expansion of West Bank settlements, praised farming outposts for âgrabbing massive territoriesâ in the region at one event where the equipment was distributed, and at another such event said the equipment was being awarded to help the outpost managers and residents “deepen our hold on the Land of Israel.”

âThe heroic and pioneering settlers who live here are doing Zionism, and they need security, they need security components, and they are not second-class citizens. We are here to build with them and to settle the land,â he said.

One incident in March this year demonstrated explicitly how this close coordination between the IDF, the government, and the settlers has affected rural Palestinians.

Video footage of the incident in the northern Jordan Valley showed a settler armed with a handgun threatening local Palestinian herders, and pointing his pistol directly at them.

The video showed that the ATV he owned still bore a sign declaring it to be a gift from the Settlements Ministry, which the settler was apparently awarded in recent months. Dror Etkes, an anti-settlement activist who monitors the movement, said it was likely the settler came from the nearby illegal farming outpost of Shirat Asavim.

âOne might think that the IDF in the West Bank is there to fight terrorism, but actually they are there to protect settlers and facilitate land grabs; this is part of the mission of the IDF,â alleged OFEK’s Shaul.

The Yesha Council, an umbrella organization representing settlement municipal councils in the West Bank, said in response that residents of agricultural and other outposts, as well as established settlements, were all “law-abiding citizens” who face terror attacks on a daily basis, including firebombs, rock-throwing, arson and agricultural theft.

“Most are terrorist attacks sponsored by the Palestinian Authority and Iran,” a spokesperson said. “Despite these relentless terror attacks, the Yesha Councilâs position has been and remains clear: Responsibility for fighting terrorism and enforcing the law rests solely with the state and the security forces.”

Yesha did not respond to The Times of Israel’s questions as to whether it condemns settler violence, and whether it will act to prevent it, especially in light of the fact that the municipal councils it represents actively participate in the establishment of illegal outposts from which much of the settler violence emanates.

Initiating friction

Since they were first established in the years following Israel’s capture of the West Bank in the 1967 Six Day War, settlements and settlers have been the target of Palestinian terrorism, including deadly infiltrations of homes and random shootings or stonings of Israeli cars on West Bank highways.

The ongoing terror threat has served not only as a rationale for expanding settlements and illegal outposts but has created a condition in which any confrontation with Palestinians brings in an IDF response, resulting at times in Palestinians being subject to violence from both settlers and soldiers who wind up abetting their illicit activity.

âOn the hilltops we say the first thing is to distance the contact line of the enemy,” Elisha Yered, a key outposts organizer, told the Hebrew-language Al Hamashmaut podcast in March. “This is a perimeter that is always going forward, otherwise it’s no use.”

âThe [livestock] herds are the tip of the spear,â he continued, in reference to the acquisition by the farming outposts of sheep and goats in order to take them out to pasture over large tracts of land as a means of asserting control and expanding the line of contact.

He explained that “instead of me going home every night and calling an emergency meeting and discussing [the Palestinians’] progress and their attempted terror attacks, they are going home every night and holding an emergency meeting about what to do about the settlers who are advancing and trying to conquer the mountain they are on at the moment.”

The outposts’ greatest period of growth has coincided with a period in which Palestinian attacks on Israelis in the West Bank have been at a low ebb, in stark contrast to settler attacks on Palestinians, which have risen sharply in recent years.

In 2025, the army recorded 1,015 stone-throwing and Molotov cocktail attacks by Palestinians, compared to 1,230 the year prior and 3,256 in 2023. In 2021, 8,633 such attacks were reported. Other types of incidents are similarly down.

According to Yered, settlers establishing and operating outposts deliberately initiate harassment and violence as a way to keep pushing out the local Palestinians from the area.

âWe are unambiguously initiating friction; we are also proud of it,â declared Yered.

When the military responds to such incidents, critics say they are most likely to end up abetting the settlers, furthering the extremists’ agenda.

âIf Yeredâs agenda is to go to [the Palestinian town of] Deir Dibwan, for example, and create friction and then have the army protect him, and if the IDFâs mission is indeed to protect these gangs, then the IDF in practice is de facto facilitating the [extremist settlersâ] mission,â charged Shaul.

A clear example of this dynamic took place in February in the Palestinian village of Mukhmas.

In an incident caught on security camera footage, settler extremists from nearby outposts, allegedly including Yered himself, entered the outskirts of Mukhmas, broke into sheep pens, let out some 350 sheep, and led them off toward the outposts. Among the settlers was the security coordinator of a nearby illegal settlement outpost who was armed with a rifle, according to reports and witnesses to the attack.

When local Palestinian men hurried to the site and tried to stop the theft, a violent confrontation broke out between the two sides.

IDF soldiers arriving at the scene dispersed the Palestinians by firing tear gas and pushing the villagers away from the area of the sheep pens, witnesses said.

Video footage of the incident published by the Haaretz news site shows the settlers and the soldiers calmly interacting during the incident, with settlers at one stage apparently directing the soldiers to the direction of the Mukhmas villagers who were trying to recover their sheep.

Mukhmas resident Nasrallah Abu Siam, 19, was killed and three villagers were injured during the incident, apparently from shots fired by settlers when the village residents tried to prevent the theft of the sheep.

Aed Abu Ali, whose family owned some of the sheep pens where thefts took place, alleged that he was beaten by the soldiers, who helped steal the sheep.

The IDF did not comment on the allegations when asked by The Times of Israel. A joint IDF and police investigation remains ongoing.

Settlers in uniform

The most serious violence carried out by IDF soldiers against Palestinian civilians has been committed by the Hagmar regional defense units.

These units were historically created to defend Israeli border communities, and comprised residents of those communities.

Following the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, most soldiers previously deployed to the West Bank were diverted to Gaza and the northern border. To take their place, the army recruited settlers to serve as reservists in regional defense units, authorizing them to operate in and around the settlements where they lived and providing them with uniforms, equipment, vehicles, and assault rifles. The total size of the network of Hagmar forces totaled some 7,000 soldiers, according to the Yesh Din organization.

The units’ operations have expanded steadily since, and their activities now include conducting patrols, setting up checkpoints, and carrying out operations inside Palestinian villages, such as searching for weapons.

Because the units are made up of local settlers, they are liable to include the same extremists responsible for setting up illegal outposts and attacking Palestinians.

Though part of the IDF’s chain of command, critics accuse the Hagmar units of acting as a rogue militia, acting on behalf of settlers but carrying the authority of IDF soldiers.

The units are often the first to arrive in response to so-called âfrictionâ in Palestinian villages, and have allegedly provided settler attackers with armed backing.

In March, an IDF reservist apparently serving in a regional defense unit shot and killed two Palestinian residents of Qaryut in the central West Bank during an incident of what the army termed “friction,” which was set off when settlers ran a backhoe through an adjacent olive grove owned by villagers.

Local Palestinians went to the area to try and stop the backhoe and threw stones at the digger, according to an IDF statement.

According to eyewitnesses cited by BâTselem, some 10 to 15 settlers then entered Qaryut itself, including the reservist soldier armed with an assault rifle, who Yesh Din says is thought to have been from a local regional defense unit

Some of the settlers began throwing stones at houses in the village, according to the BâTselem investigation, and when Palestinian residents began to throw stones at the settlers, the regional defense soldier shot Muhammad Muammar, 52, in the head, and his brother Fahim Muammar, 47, in the pelvis while they were standing outside the gate to Muhammadâs house.

???? Happening now: Settler terrorists opened live fire, killing two brothers inside their home in Qaryut village near Nablus. Reports indicate the terrorists are still in the village while the IDF stands by. Iran? Lebanon? Nothing stops ethnic cleansing from moving forward. pic.twitter.com/sIw1mMGpLX — Breaking the Silence (@BtSIsrael) March 2, 2026

Muhammad, a father of six children, and Fahim, a father of five, were both killed. A third brother was also shot by the same soldier, but survived, while a 15-year-old was shot and injured by a different settler.

The IDF has opened an investigation into the incident and confiscated the soldierâs rifle.

According to Yesh Din, of 12 Palestinians killed by settlers so far this year, seven were killed by Hagmar unit soldiers.

The units have also been frequently involved in harassment and vandalism against Palestinians.

In one incident in March 2025, settler extremists attacked the village of Jinba and severely beat and injured three villagers, following a confrontation between settlers and villagers earlier in the day.

A regional defense unit arrived in Jinba after the settler attack, arrested 22 men and boys from the village on suspicion of involvement in the earlier confrontation, handcuffed and blindfolded them, and took them to a nearby military base.

The IDF declined to comment at the time as to whether any of the settlers involved in the assault on Jinba had been arrested.

The regional defense unit returned to Jinba after midnight and ransacked a dwelling, destroying produce made by villagers such as yogurt, butter, and olive oil, vandalized an Italian-funded school, and rampaged through Jinbaâs clinic, damaging infrastructure and medical facilities.

The IDF disciplined several officers and troops for vandalizing property during the incident, after an investigation into the affair.

Meinrath said he had seen Hagmar soldiers harass Palestinian farmers and prevent them from carrying out agricultural work. In other cases, he said, the regional defense troops stood by as extremists set fire to harvests or stole produce, sometimes actively shielding the settlers.

âUsually the regional defense units protect the settlers and allow them to do whatever they want,â said the activist.

For volunteer Gur, the problem is not confined to regional defense units or even just the army. Rather, she contended, the abuse being suffered by rural Palestinians is a reflection of the nation’s attitude.

âWe used to say the army is the face of our society, and unfortunately, that is true today as well,â she said despondently. âSaying it is only one battalion, one division — no, no, no. This is the face of the army all over the place and this is the face of society.”

The Yesha Council requested that its entire response, which references the incidents in Mukhmas, Jinba, and Turmus Ayya, be included in full:

“The attempt to base a broad claim on three isolated incidents over a period of nearly a year and a half, incidents for which the full factual context was not even presented, does not reflect the reality in Judea and Samaria.

“The reality on the ground is that the residents of the agricultural farms, as well as those in both the new and established communities, are law-abiding citizens. Every single day, they face terror attacks. From rock-throwing, Molotov cocktails, to arson and agricultural theft. Most are terrorist attacks sponsored by the Palestinian Authority and Iran.

“Despite these relentless terror attacks, the Yesha Councilâs position has been and remains clear: Responsibility for fighting terrorism and enforcing the law rests solely with the state and the security forces.

“The Yesha Council will continue to build, develop, and settle the land of our ancestors, and no attempt to present a distorted reality in Judea and Samaria will deter us from our path.”

World.title: US considering moving Gulf bases hit by Iran westward, including to Israel — report
World.content:
The United States is considering moving Middle East military installations westward, including to Israel, to reduce their exposure to Iran’s missiles and drones, which dealt the region’s sole US Navy base some $400 million in damage largely unacknowledged by the Pentagon, the Wall Street Journal reported Thursday.

Tehran’s retaliatory strikes, following the start of the US-Israeli bombing campaign in Iran on February 28, hit US military installations across the region, killing 13 servicemembers and wounding hundreds.

Buildings harmed at the Naval Support Activity Bahrain (NSA Bahrain) base, which lies some 240 kilometers (150 miles) south of Iran, include the Fifth Fleet headquarters, a barracks, several warehouses and a potable water tank, the Journal said Thursday, citing satellite and social media images.

No one was killed at the base, according to the US military, the Journal said.

The outlet said it estimated the cost of the damages based on procurement reports and the Pentagon’s publicly available cost model.

Get The Times of Israel's Daily Edition by email and never miss our top stories Newsletter email address Get it By signing up, you agree to the terms

The estimate included only construction costs, the Journal said. It cited an analyst with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think tank as saying that, depending on what the buildings housed, that estimate could end up being dwarfed by other costs of the damage. For example, according to CSIS, two satellite communication terminals that Iran destroyed early in the war cost some $20 million each, the report said.

The damage to NSA Bahrain has led the US to weigh revamping the base, including by moving command centers underground and passing on rebuilding some of the destroyed structures, according to US officials familiar with the deliberations who were cited by the Journal.

The US may also curb its presence in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, and shift some of it westward, following Iran’s targeting of military installations in the two Arab states, the officials said.



The U.S. Navy base in Bahrain was repeatedly targeted between late February and June. Strikes that got through caused extensive damage, according to a Wall Street Journal analysis of satellite imagery, social-media footage and interviews with current and formerâ¦ — Lara Seligman (@laraseligman) June 26, 2026

According to two of the officials, one of the destinations being weighed is Israel, where dozens of US jets parked at Ben Gurion Airport since the lead-up to the Iran war have stymied Israelis’ travel.

US President Donald Trump has faced fierce criticism in the US, including within his own Republican party, over the spiraling cost of the Iran war, which also sparked a global spike in energy prices after Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for oil shipments.

Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth is seeking roughly $80 billion in supplemental funding to shore up defense supplies in the aftermath of the war, which entered a truce on April 8.

The US and Iran last week reached a memorandum of understanding that kicked off 60 days of negotiations to end hostilities across the region.



Israel is not a party to the MOU or the negotiations, and Israeli officials have criticized the agreement, which requires a halt to Israel’s operations against Iran’s Lebanese proxy Hezbollah, and contains no concrete concessions from Iran on its nuclear program.

Agencies contributed to this report.

World.title: Vetting panel disqualifies heritage minister’s nominee for Antiquities Authority chief
World.content:
A governmental vetting committee on Thursday nixed Heritage Minister Amichay Eliyahu’s nominee to lead the Israel Antiquities Authority.

Hebrew media reported the committee, led by retired judge Shulamit Dotan, blocked Esther Schreiber because the tender that led to Schreiber’s selection in May featured lower criteria than demanded by law.

Haaretz cited sources who had seen the decision as saying Schreiber failed to satisfy the legal requirements to be IAA director, which, under Israel’s 1975 Government Companies Law, include five years of senior managerial experience.

The newspaper and other outlets previously reported that Schreiber had significantly embellished her resume, including by exaggerating the size of a religious advocacy organization she managed.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, head of Eliyahu’s far-right Otzma Yehudit party, claimed the “deep state” had blocked Schreiber because she is visibly observant.

Get The Times of Israel's Daily Edition by email and never miss our top stories Newsletter email address Get it By signing up, you agree to the terms

“The official reason — legal. The real reason — a religious CEO with a head covering doesn’t sit right with the deep state,” Ben Gvir wrote on X.

The High Court earlier this month declined to block Schreiber’s appointment. Ahead of a hearing on the matter, Eliyahu sent Justice Yechiel Kasher a highly unusual text message asking him “to help safeguard our right — and our duty — to implement the policy for which we were elected.” The judge panned the minister over the move.

Schreiber, like the current IAA head Eli Escozido and his predecessor, Israel Hasson, does not have a background in archaeology.



Her selection for IAA chief came as the government sought to establish a separate antiquities authority, also under the Heritage Ministry, to oversee archaeological activities in the West Bank and Gaza. Critics in Israeli academia and the Palestinian Authority have said the effort amounts to de facto annexation, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly halted the legislative process earlier this month amid the controversy.

Rosella Tercatin contributed to this report.

World.title: Massachusetts principal under fire for apologizing for antisemitism discussion
World.content:
JTA — A lesson on antisemitism went awry after the principal of a Boston-area middle school sent an obliquely worded apology letter to parents this week.

The incident at William Diamond Middle School in Lexington, Massachusetts, initially prompted some Jewish social media accounts and conservative US news outlets to conclude the principal, Dr. Johnny Cole, was apologizing for teaching about the Holocaust.

A local media outlet, however, reported Thursday that Cole’s apology was not related to the Holocaust at all. Rather, he had apologized for a lesson on modern-day antisemitism that the school had contracted a local third-party Jewish group to teach.

Following the lesson, the Lexington Observer reported that a dozen families had objected to the group’s use of material from the Blue Square Alliance, an antisemitism advocacy and monitoring organization, because its founder, New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, is a prominent supporter of Israel. This prompted Cole to write “we are sorry” to students who, he wrote, “felt like your own history, your identity, or your community was left out or erased.”

Cole continued: “Every one of you deserves to walk into this school and feel that who you are matters — Arab students; Jewish students; Lebanese students; Muslim students; Palestinian students — every student.” Lexington Observer verified and published his apology.
